Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that put my body under stress
I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

vignette:
Mina, a 25-year-old South Eastern Asian woman who worked as a database administrator, came to treatment after a year in which her life had narrowed around a single night on a rain-slick highway. She and her husband had been driving home when another car drifted across lanes and hit them with such force that the cabin spun, glass exploded, and the metallic smell of the wreck filled the air. In the moments before the collision she had been arguing with her husband about an ordinary household matter, and that detail had lodged in her mind as if it explained everything that followed. In the weeks afterward, she found herself seizing on the smallest reminders: hearing a name that sounded like the other driver's or even a family member's name could tighten her chest and pull her back to the crash; arguments in the apartment made her feel cornered and unsafe; uncertainty of any kind, even a delayed text message or an unclear work instruction, felt unbearable because it evoked the helplessness of not knowing what was coming next. What frightened Mina most was how quickly these moments turned into certainty in her mind that she had somehow caused the event by the way she acted, and that she had not done enough to stop it. She replayed the seconds before impact and became convinced she would never forgive herself for not doing more, and she started to think that people could not be trusted at all if danger could appear so suddenly and no one could prevent it.

As those interpretations hardened, Mina's daily life became organized around keeping herself from feeling that surge of fear and blame again. She stopped seeing friends, first cancelling dinners and then declining invitations altogether, because conversations could drift into stories about driving, weather, or other people's accidents, and she did not trust herself to stay composed. She avoided physical stress of any kind, stepping away from anything that made her body feel taxed or shaky, because a racing heart or tense muscles reminded her too much of the crash and made her feel as if another catastrophe was imminent. On especially bad evenings, when the memory would not stop circling, she hurt herself physically to interrupt the thoughts and to force her attention away from the event. She described those moments not as wanting death, but as needing something more immediate than memory, something she could control when her mind would not. Over time, these strategies shrank her world and made her more alone, and the loneliness gave her more room to think about how badly she believed she had failed. The less she saw people, the more certain she became that they could not be trusted; the more she avoided strain and ordinary social life, the more she felt weak, guilty, and responsible for what had happened. Even at work, where she sat for hours in front of database screens, she began to dread any situation that demanded quick judgment or physical effort, and she would tense whenever a coworker raised their voice nearby, as though another argument might mean another disaster.

The same coping habits also kept bringing the danger back into view. By arranging her days around avoidance, Mina became exquisitely alert to anything that might intrude on those routines: a colleague mentioning a familiar-sounding name, a spouse's raised voice in the next room, the uncertainty of not knowing whether she could get through the workday without becoming overwhelmed. Because she was constantly trying to ward off reminders, she noticed them everywhere, and each new jolt confirmed her belief that she was still unsafe and somehow at fault. She had come to see her self-harm, her retreat from friends, and her refusal of physical strain as the only ways to keep herself steady, yet each one left her more exposed to the very thoughts she feared, and more convinced that she could not trust herself or other people. By the time she sought help, Mina was exhausted by the cycle and increasingly afraid that the pattern was becoming permanent. She came to therapy hoping to stop living as if the crash were happening again every day, and what she feared most was that she would remain trapped in guilt, mistrust, and the need to hurt herself just to get through a thought.
